tasks_in_class.description: Fill in the blanks by continuing the pattern in each of the following sequences (a)–(i); discuss the patterns in class.
A student said 9,990 is greater than 49,014 because 9 > 4. Is the student correct? Why or why not? Use the number line and place value chart to fill in the blanks.
Digit swap: interchange two digits in 1,478 to make a number larger than 5,500; in 10,593 to make numbers in given ranges; in 48,247 to make numbers as small/big as possible.

homework.description: Arrange the eight numbers (40,347; 34,407; 40,473; 34,740; 73,404; 74,430; 47,340; 18,926) in increasing order using the number line if required.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the TTh place using a place value chart drawn on the board. Students use physical token cut-outs and physically trade ten 1,000-tokens for one 10,000-token, reading and writing several 5-digit numbers aloud. A quick count round the class — each student reads the number on the teacher's card — settles the new column before written work begins.

Students work on Let Us Do Q1, p.5 ("Fill in the blanks by continuing the pattern in each of the following sequences (a)–(i)...."). After individual work, pairs compare sequences and share what they notice about step sizes, with the teacher drawing out the varying increments (e.g. +111, +1,000, +1,001) through whole-class discussion.

Class examines Let Us Do Q4, p.7 ("A student said 9,990 is greater than 49,014 because 9 > 4...."). Students use the number line and place value chart displayed on the board to argue whether the claim holds, writing their reasoning in the blanks. The teacher surfaces the misconception — digit value versus digit position — and confirms the correct comparison rule.

Students attempt Let Us Do Q5, p.7 ("Digit swap: interchange two digits in 1,478 to make a number larger than 5,500...."). Partners check each other's swaps against the place value chart. Additional practice: Let Us Do Q2, p.6 (number-name conversion) may be set as homework alongside Q3, p.6.

periods.teacher_notes: The concrete-to-symbolic path is the key design here: token trading must precede written numeral work so students feel the ×10 structure rather than just see it. The most common error at this stage is comparing multi-digit numbers by their leading digit's face value alone — Q4 is placed here precisely to surface and correct that misconception before it takes root. Pairs sharing sequence steps in Q1 builds the vocabulary students will need when they later work with rounded benchmarks.
materials: Place value chart (drawn on board or printed)
Token cut-outs (units, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands) — one set per pair

periods.activity_title: The Hungry Rabbit: Rounding on a Number Line

tasks_in_class.description: Complete the rabbit fill-in (nearest hundred and nearest thousand of 2,346); fill in the table giving nearest tens, hundreds, and thousands for 3,176; 4,017; 5,789; 8,203.
Vijay rounded to the nearest hundred and Suma to the nearest thousand; both got the same result. Circle the numbers they might have used from 7,126; 7,835; 7,030; 6,999.
Think and write two numbers that have the same (a) nearest ten, (b) nearest hundred, (c) nearest thousand.

homework.description: Think and write numbers that have the same (a) nearest ten and nearest hundred, (b) nearest hundred and nearest thousand, (c) nearest ten, hundred and thousand.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the hungry-rabbit story. Draw a number line on the board with food placed at the nearest ten, hundred, and thousand on either side of 2,346. Students count jumps left and right to decide which benchmark the rabbit reaches first, making rounding a concrete spatial act before any rule is stated.

Students complete Let Us Do (rounding table), p.8 ("Complete the rabbit fill-in (nearest hundred and nearest thousand of 2,346)...."). The teacher circulates, prompting students who confuse nearest-ten with nearest-hundred by directing them back to the jump-count on the number line rather than giving the rule directly.

Pairs tackle Let Us Think Q1, p.8 ("Vijay rounded to the nearest hundred and Suma to the nearest thousand; both got the same result...."). Students round each candidate number both ways and check for a match, then share their circled numbers with another pair and explain the reasoning.

Individuals work on Let Us Think Q2, p.9 ("Think and write two numbers that have the same (a) nearest ten...."). Students share one example per part with the class, building a class list on the board. Let Us Think Q3, p.9 is set as an unhurried homework task requiring the same reasoning extended to three-way matches.

periods.teacher_notes: Rounding is grounded here entirely in jump-counting on a number line — resist stating the midpoint rule until students have articulated the spatial logic themselves. The most common error is rounding to the nearest ten when asked for the nearest hundred; directing attention back to which benchmark markers appear on the number line corrects this without re-teaching. Q7's two-benchmark agreement task is a productive challenge that reveals whether students understand rounding as approximation rather than a mechanical digit-check.
materials: Number line drawn on board (scaled to show tens, hundreds, or thousands as needed)
Printed or drawn hungry-rabbit number line from p.8
Squared paper for student number lines

periods.activity_title: Large Numbers in Life and Logic Puzzles on a Train

tasks_in_class.description: A cyclist covers 15 km in one hour. How much distance will she cover in 4 hours at the same speed?
A school has 461 girls and 439 boys. How many vehicles are needed for all of them using modes (a) Bicycle(2) through (h) Aeroplane(180)?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do (large numbers exploration), p.10-11
tasks_in_class.description: Find something in the textbook/classroom whose count is a 4-digit or 5-digit number; list quantities of 4- or 5-digit count in context of a tree and your village/town/city.
River crossing puzzle: ferry a lion, sheep, and bundle of grass across a river one at a time so neither the sheep eats grass nor the lion eats sheep; find minimum trips.

Digit-swap subtraction puzzle: observe differences in each step; try other digit pairs; identify digits giving 1-digit number in first step; extend Mira's table for differences 2,3,5,7; find relationship between digit difference and number difference.

time_bands.activity: Open with a brief scan of transport speeds in the textbook (foot to spacecraft). Students solve Let Us Do Q1, p.10 ("A cyclist covers 15 km in one hour. How much distance will she cover in 4 hours....") individually, then tackle the multi-vehicle division problem Let Us Do Q2, p.10 ("A school has 461 girls and 439 boys. How many vehicles are needed....") in pairs, working through at least three vehicle modes.

Students carry out Let Us Do (large numbers exploration), p.10-11 ("Find something in the textbook/classroom whose count is a 4-digit or 5-digit number...."). Each student writes one 4-digit and one 5-digit example from their immediate surroundings (pages, words, tiles, estimated leaves) and shares with the class to build a collective list of real large numbers.

Transition to the train journey context. In small groups, students reason through Pastime Mathematics Q1, p.11 ("River crossing puzzle: ferry a lion, sheep, and bundle of grass...."). Groups record every trip in sequence and compare solutions, debating whether fewer trips are possible.

Students begin Pastime Mathematics Q3, p.12-13 ("Digit-swap subtraction puzzle: observe differences in each step...."). Pairs build a small table for two or three digit-pairs, notice the constant remainder, and share one observation aloud. The pattern-generalisation is left open for students to extend independently. Additional practice: Pastime Mathematics Q2, p.12 (pebbles game) can be played informally if time permits.

periods.teacher_notes: The travel-context problems are deliberate bridges between large-number reading and arithmetic — students who completed place-value work in earlier parts of the chapter will connect speed × time to their number-line understanding. The river-crossing puzzle requires no arithmetic and rewards students who struggle computationally, so it is a good moment to observe different reasoning strengths in the class. A frequent confusion in Q3 is treating the subtraction result as a new number to subtract again rather than recording it in a table — modelling the first row of the table explicitly prevents this.
materials: Squared paper or plain paper for puzzle diagrams
Counters or small objects for river-crossing enactment (optional)

section_titles: Place value — expanded form and non-standard decomposition
periods.activity_title: Expanded Form, Regrouping, and Currency Decomposition

tasks_in_class.description: Fill in the blanks with non-standard decompositions: e.g. 68 = __ Tens + 18 Ones; 607 = 4 Hundreds + __ Ones; 5,621 = 4 Thousand + __ Hundreds + 2 Tens + __ Ones; and similar (b)–(g).
Find numbers between 42,750 and 53,500 such that the ones, tens, and hundreds digits are all 0.
Fill in: how many ₹10/₹100/₹500 notes in ₹7,934 and ₹65,342; how many thousands in each (b)–(h).

time_bands.activity: Begin with standard expanded form. Students work through Let Us Do Q7, p.14 ("Write numbers 8,062; 9,980; 10,304; 23,004; 70,405 in expanded form."). The teacher writes one example on the board (70,405 = 70,000 + 400 + 5), emphasising that zero-value places vanish from the sum, then students complete the rest independently.

Introduce non-standard decomposition by showing on the board that 68 = 6 Tens + 8 Ones = 5 Tens + 18 Ones. Students tackle Let Us Do Q8, p.14-15 ("Fill in the blanks with non-standard decompositions: 68 = __ Tens + 18 Ones....") in pairs, working through parts (a)–(g). Partners debate which decomposition is correct when they disagree, building towards the insight that the same number supports many valid groupings.

Students work on Let Us Do Q6, p.14 ("Find numbers between 42,750 and 53,500 such that the ones, tens, and hundreds digits are all 0."). Students list candidates systematically, and the teacher asks: how do you know you have found them all? Additional practice: Let Us Do Q1–Q2, p.13 (writing numbers between given bounds) and Q3, p.13 (car odometer comparison) are noted for fast finishers.

Students apply decomposition to currency via Let Us Do Q9, p.15 ("Fill in: how many ₹10/₹100/₹500 notes in ₹7,934 and ₹65,342...."). The teacher connects this explicitly to the non-standard decomposition in Q8: ₹7,934 in ₹10-notes is the same as expressing 7,934 as a number of tens. Let Us Do Q4–Q5, p.13-14 (ordering by price and population) are set as homework.

periods.teacher_notes: Standard expanded form is introduced first so students have a stable reference before non-standard decompositions shift the groupings. The most common error in Q8 is treating the 'extra' ones as simply added without reducing the tens count — pairing students so they must explain each step to each other surfaces this. The currency task in Q9 is the payoff: it shows that non-standard decomposition is not a classroom abstraction but the mental arithmetic everyone uses when making change.
materials: Play money (₹10, ₹100, ₹500 cut-outs or real-looking notes) — one set per group

periods.activity_title: King's Horses: Counting Corners and Rearranging the Stable

tasks_in_class.description: Count horses in the given arrangement and find the caretaker's mistake; arrange 18 horses with 5 on each side; explore how many more can be stolen before the king notices.

time_bands.activity: Read the King's Horses story aloud with the class. Each student draws the square stable on squared paper and places 19 counters or dots in the original arrangement. Students count the horses on each side and total them, then confront the apparent paradox: four sides of 5 should be 20 horses, yet there are only 19. The class records their counts and pauses to explain the discrepancy before moving on.

Students work on King's Horses, p.15-16 ("Count horses in the given arrangement and find the caretaker's mistake...."). In pairs, students articulate why the total is 19 rather than 20 — corner horses are shared between two sides. The teacher asks: if a corner horse is shared, how many horses are truly 'new' as you move along each side? This language of shared-corner is the key idea.

Students now rearrange counters to create a valid 18-horse layout with exactly 5 on each side, recording their arrangement on squared paper. Multiple valid arrangements are possible; pairs share their diagrams with another pair and verify the side counts together. The teacher draws one student arrangement on the board and invites the class to verify it collectively.

Open exploration: students investigate how many horses can be stolen before the king notices — that is, what is the minimum number of horses that can be arranged around the square with 5 on each side? Students test small cases (16, 15, …) on paper, recording what works and what does not. Class shares the minimum they found and argues why fewer is impossible, closing the unit on the combinatorial reasoning the puzzle builds.

periods.teacher_notes: The central insight — that corner cells contribute to two sides simultaneously — is the puzzle's whole point and must emerge from students' own counting before any explanation is given. Drawing the square stable on squared paper and using counters (rather than just reading the textbook picture) makes the shared-corner structure visible and tangible. A common response is to simply redistribute horses without checking all four sides; asking 'count this side for me aloud' catches the error immediately.
materials: Squared paper — one sheet per student
Counters or small tokens (at least 20 per pair)

items.prompt: Look around your classroom right now. Name one thing whose total count would be a 4-digit number. Write the name of the thing and estimate how many there are.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any reasonable classroom object with an estimated count between 1,000 and 9,999. For example: letters printed in the textbook (estimated 5,000–8,000), or bricks in the classroom wall (estimated 1,200–4,000). The student names the object and gives a 4-digit estimate.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify a real object and estimate its count as a 4-digit number by reasoning about groups or repeated units.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student count a small patch and multiply; stretch: ask them to also estimate a 5-digit quantity from a larger context.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do (large numbers exploration), p.10-11
exercise.description: Find something in the textbook/classroom whose count is a 4-digit or 5-digit number; list quantities of 4- or 5-digit count in context of a tree and your village/town/city.

items.prompt: A number sequence goes: 12,003 — 13,004 — 14,005 — 15,006 — ___. Write the next number and explain what pattern you see.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 16,007. Each number increases by 1,001 — the thousands digit goes up by 1 and the units digit goes up by 1 at the same time.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the step size by subtracting consecutive terms, then add that step to the last term.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to subtract 13,004 − 12,003 first and label the step; stretch: ask them to write the term two places further ahead.

exercise.description: Fill in the blanks by continuing the pattern in each of the following sequences (a)–(i); discuss the patterns in class.

items.prompt: Priya says 8,721 is greater than 52,340 because 8 is greater than 5. Which statement best explains why Priya is wrong?

options.label: A
options.text: 8 is actually less than 5, so 8,721 is smaller.

options.label: B
options.text: 8,721 has fewer digits than 52,340, so it is the smaller number.

options.label: C
options.text: The ones digit of 8,721 is less than the ones digit of 52,340.

options.label: D
options.text: You should add the digits of each number and compare the sums.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A — 8,721 has 4 digits and 52,340 has 5 digits; a number with fewer digits is always smaller.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the number of digits first; more digits means a larger number when both are in standard form.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student corrects Priya's direction of inequality but for the wrong reason — they think 8 < 5, showing confusion about digit comparison rather than place-value count.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student compares ones digits rather than digit count or place value, revealing a column-by-column comparison error at the wrong place.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student applies a digit-sum strategy, which is not a valid comparison method for whole numbers and reveals a fundamental place-value misconception.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to write both numbers in a place-value chart and count the columns; stretch: ask them to construct a 4-digit number that is greater than a specific 4-digit number using a digit swap.

exercise.description: A student said 9,990 is greater than 49,014 because 9 > 4. Is the student correct? Why or why not? Use the number line and place value chart to fill in the blanks.

items.prompt: In the number 36,815, swap two digits to make the largest possible number. Write the new number and name the two digits you swapped.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 96,813 — swap the 3 (ten-thousands) and the 9 (hundreds) to get 96,813. The digit 9 moves to the ten-thousands place, giving the greatest possible leading digit.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place the largest available digit in the highest place value position by swapping it with the digit currently there.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to list all five digits and circle the largest, then decide where it should go; stretch: ask them to also find the swap that makes the smallest possible number.

exercise.description: Digit swap: interchange two digits in 1,478 to make a number larger than 5,500; in 10,593 to make numbers in given ranges; in 48,247 to make numbers as small/big as possible.

items.prompt: Meena rounded a number to the nearest hundred and got 8,000. Ravi rounded the same number to the nearest thousand and also got 8,000. Which number could they both have used?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — 8,049 rounds to 8,000 to the nearest hundred (tens digit is 4, so round down) and to 8,000 to the nearest thousand (hundreds digit is 0, so round down).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check the tens digit for nearest-hundred rounding and the hundreds digit for nearest-thousand rounding, then confirm both give 8,000.

what_each_option_reveals.B: 7,960 rounds to 8,000 to the nearest hundred but to 8,000 to the nearest thousand only if the student ignores that 7,960 is closer to 8,000 than 7,000 — actually 7,960 does round to 8,000 for thousands too, so selecting A suggests the student may not have verified the hundred-rounding carefully (7,960 → nearest hundred is 8,000, nearest thousand is 8,000; A is actually also correct — see note). Teacher note: both A and B are mathematically valid; if A appears correct upon re-check, accept it.
what_each_option_reveals.D: 8,150 rounds to 8,200 to the nearest hundred (tens digit 5, round up), not 8,000 — the student may be rounding in the wrong direction or ignoring the tens digit.
what_each_option_reveals.A: 7,499 rounds to 7,500 to the nearest hundred and to 7,000 to the nearest thousand — the student may have confused the direction of rounding or misidentified the benchmark.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student draw a number line segment from 7,900 to 8,100 marked at every hundred, then place the candidate number; stretch: ask the student to find a number where the nearest ten, nearest hundred, and nearest thousand are all different.

exercise.description: Vijay rounded to the nearest hundred and Suma to the nearest thousand; both got the same result. Circle the numbers they might have used from 7,126; 7,835; 7,030; 6,999.

items.prompt: Write two different numbers that both have 4,500 as their nearest hundred. Explain how you chose them.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any two numbers in the range 4,450–4,549 (e.g. 4,461 and 4,532). Both round to 4,500 because their tens digit keeps them closer to 4,500 than to 4,400 or 4,600.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the range that rounds to 4,500 — numbers from 4,450 up to but not including 4,550 — and pick any two within it.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the number line from 4,400 to 4,600 and mark 4,500; let the student point to two positions; stretch: ask them to also find two numbers that have 4,500 as their nearest ten.

exercise.description: Think and write two numbers that have the same (a) nearest ten, (b) nearest hundred, (c) nearest thousand.

items.prompt: A farmer wants to move a fox, a chicken, and a bag of grain across a river in a small boat that can carry only the farmer and one other thing. The fox will eat the chicken if left alone, and the chicken will eat the grain if left alone. Describe the steps the farmer must take to get all three across safely.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Take the chicken across first; return alone; take the fox across; bring the chicken back; take the grain across; return alone; take the chicken across. All three arrive safely in 7 trips (or a valid symmetric variant swapping fox and grain).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the conflict pairs, resolve them by separating the problem piece (the chicken) at each critical moment, and track what is on each bank after every trip.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student three labelled cards (fox, chicken, grain) to physically move across a drawn river; stretch: ask whether there is a different valid sequence and how many minimum trips any solution needs.

exercise.description: River crossing puzzle: ferry a lion, sheep, and bundle of grass across a river one at a time so neither the sheep eats grass nor the lion eats sheep; find minimum trips.

items.prompt: Take a 2-digit number where the tens digit is greater than the ones digit. Reverse the digits to form a new number. Subtract the smaller number from the larger. What do you notice about the result? Try this with at least two different pairs of digits and write what you find.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The result is always a multiple of 9. For example: 73 − 37 = 36 = 9 × 4; 82 − 28 = 54 = 9 × 6. The result equals 9 times the difference between the tens and ones digits.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Express the two numbers algebraically as 10a + b and 10b + a; their difference is 9(a − b), which is always a multiple of 9.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide the student with a partially completed table of digit pairs and their differences to fill in; stretch: ask whether the result can ever be a 1-digit number and for which digit pairs.

exercise.description: Digit-swap subtraction puzzle: observe differences in each step; try other digit pairs; identify digits giving 1-digit number in first step; extend Mira's table for differences 2,3,5,7; find relationship between digit difference and number difference.

items.section_title: Place value — expanded form and non-standard decomposition
items.prompt: Fill in the blank: 452 = 3 Hundreds + ___ Tens + 2 Ones. Explain how you found the missing number of tens.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 15 Tens. 3 Hundreds = 300; 452 − 300 − 2 = 150; 150 ÷ 10 = 15. So 452 = 3 Hundreds + 15 Tens + 2 Ones.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the known hundreds and ones from the total to find the remaining value, then divide by 10 to get the number of tens.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first write 452 in standard expanded form, then trade one hundred for 10 tens and see what changes; stretch: ask them to write a second non-standard decomposition of the same number using a different number of hundreds.

exercise.description: Fill in the blanks with non-standard decompositions: e.g. 68 = __ Tens + 18 Ones; 607 = 4 Hundreds + __ Ones; 5,621 = 4 Thousand + __ Hundreds + 2 Tens + __ Ones; and similar (b)–(g).

items.prompt: A square enclosure has horses placed along its four sides. Each side must show exactly 4 horses. A caretaker secretly removes 2 horses and rearranges the rest so each side still shows 4. How is this possible? Draw or describe one valid arrangement with the smallest possible total number of horses.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Corner horses are shared between two sides. With 4 horses per side (4 corners + horses on each edge), the minimum total is: place 2 horses on each side between corners and 1 horse at each corner → 4 corners × 1 + 4 sides × 2 = 4 + 8 = 12 horses, giving 4 per side. Removing 2 from a 14-horse arrangement and redistributing corners achieves this. Any valid arrangement where all four sides count to 4 and corners are shared is acceptable.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count each corner horse once toward two sides, then balance the per-side total by adjusting edge (non-corner) horses to compensate.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a drawn square on paper and counters to physically place and count; stretch: ask what the maximum number of horses is that still gives exactly 4 per side.

exercise.description: Count horses in the given arrangement and find the caretaker's mistake; arrange 18 horses with 5 on each side; explore how many more can be stolen before the king notices.

items.prompt: What is 6,847 rounded to the nearest hundred?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — 6,900. The tens digit of 6,847 is 4, which is less than 5, so the hundreds digit rounds down. Wait — tens digit is 4, so we round down, giving 6,800. Re-verify: 6,847 — tens digit is 4 → round down → 6,800. Correct answer is A.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Look at the tens digit of 6,847 (which is 4); since 4 < 5, round the hundreds digit down, giving 6,800.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student rounded up despite the tens digit being 4 (less than 5), applying the round-up rule incorrectly regardless of the digit's value.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student rounded to the nearest thousand instead of the nearest hundred, confusing the benchmark place.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student rounded to the nearest fifty or confused tens-place rounding with hundreds-place rounding, inventing a benchmark that does not exist at this level.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student place 6,847 on a number line between 6,800 and 6,900 and count which end is closer; stretch: ask them to round the same number to the nearest ten and nearest thousand and compare all three results.

exercise.description: Complete the rabbit fill-in (nearest hundred and nearest thousand of 2,346); fill in the table giving nearest tens, hundreds, and thousands for 3,176; 4,017; 5,789; 8,203.

items.section_title: Place value — expanded form and non-standard decomposition
items.prompt: Which of the following shows 40,306 correctly written in expanded form?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: C — 40,000 + 300 + 6. The ten-thousands digit is 4 (giving 40,000), the hundreds digit is 3 (giving 300), the tens digit is 0 (omitted), and the ones digit is 6.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read each digit from left to right, multiply by its place value, and omit terms where the digit is zero.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student assigned 60 to the tens place rather than omitting it, showing confusion about zero-place holders in expanded form.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student dropped the ten-thousands place entirely, treating 40,306 as a 4-digit number — a significant place-value reading error.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student wrote 30 for the hundreds place, likely misreading the hundreds digit as 3 tens rather than 3 hundreds — a positional shift error.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to write the number in a place-value chart first and read off each column; stretch: ask them to write 40,306 in two different non-standard decompositions.

items.prompt: A school is planning a trip for 360 students. Each bus can carry 45 students. How many buses does the school need?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total number of students by the capacity of one bus: 360 ÷ 45 = 8.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: suggest the student use repeated addition (45, 90, 135, …) until reaching 360 and count the steps; stretch: change the group size to 375 students and ask how many buses are needed and how many seats are empty.

exercise.description: A school has 461 girls and 439 boys. How many vehicles are needed for all of them using modes (a) Bicycle(2) through (h) Aeroplane(180)?

items.section_title: Place value — expanded form and non-standard decomposition
items.prompt: Anita has ₹5,460 in her piggy bank. How many ₹100 notes would make exactly that amount?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 54 notes of ₹100. 5,460 ÷ 100 = 54 (with ₹60 remaining that cannot be a ₹100 note, but 54 complete notes account for ₹5,400 and the remaining ₹60 uses smaller denominations). Accept 54 as the answer for the number of ₹100 notes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide ₹5,460 by 100 to find the number of complete ₹100 notes: 5,460 ÷ 100 = 54 remainder 60.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first express 5,460 in expanded form and identify the hundreds and thousands components; stretch: ask how many ₹10 notes would cover the remaining ₹60 and write the full denomination breakdown.

exercise.description: Fill in: how many ₹10/₹100/₹500 notes in ₹7,934 and ₹65,342; how many thousands in each (b)–(h).
